strengths: Introduces a novel multi-modal diffusion-based data generation pipeline that jointly extracts FLUX DiT feature maps, concept-attention maps, and DINO-v3 features to decode high-quality masks directly from the generative process, avoiding the performance ceiling of relying on an external teacher segmentation model.

Produces a large-scale (139k image) high-resolution synthetic SOD dataset (S3OD) that is more than 2x the size of all existing SOD datasets combined, with a multi-stage quality-filtering pipeline (consistency, VLM-based mask quality, semantic validation) and demonstrated low synthetic-to-real domain gap via UMAP and precision/recall analysis against real distributions.
Proposes an iterative, feedback-driven generation framework that reweights category sampling based on per-category model performance, with ablations showing consistent gains across rounds.

Ambiguity-aware multi-mask decoder architecture is well-motivated, simple, and ablated (backbone choice, number of mask branches, auxiliary loss regularization/decay), addressing a genuine limitation of prior single-output SOD models.

Extensive empirical evaluation: cross-dataset generalization across six SOD/DIS benchmarks, fine-tuned SOTA comparisons, retraining of existing baselines (BiRefNet, MVANet) on S3OD to isolate dataset effect, comparison to other synthetic-data generation methods (MaskFactory, DatasetDM), zero-shot and fine-tuned transfer to camouflaged object detection, and comparisons with SAM-based pipelines and model efficiency (FLOPs/FPS).

Comprehensive appendix with feature-complementarity visualizations, prompt-generation analysis, dataset quality metrics (IS/FID), and thorough ablations, indicating good experimental rigor and transparency about limitations.
weaknesses: No held-out test split is released for S3OD (explicitly acknowledged), which limits its future use as a standardized benchmark and makes some internal evaluations (e.g., category feedback scoring) harder to verify independently.

The pipeline depends on several large proprietary/closed components (FLUX-Krea, GPT-4 for prompt generation, Gemma-3 VLM for filtering), which raises reproducibility concerns as these models evolve or become inaccessible, and makes exact replication costly.

Some reported gains (e.g., 'up to 50% error reduction') are best-case numbers from selected comparisons rather than consistent average improvements; the actual per-benchmark gains vary substantially (e.g., some DUT-OMRON or UHRSD improvements are much more modest), so headline claims may overstate typical performance.

The multi-mask decoder ablation (Table 15) shows only small numerical differences across configurations, and given the limited grid search (four hand-picked configurations due to compute cost), the robustness/significance of the specific λ_reg/γ choice is not strongly established.

The 'S3OD*' oracle (best-of-three-masks) evaluation, while appropriately caveated as not directly comparable, is still used to support the ambiguity-aware architecture narrative without a more rigorous multi-hypothesis evaluation metric (e.g., generalized energy distance) or human-annotated ambiguity ground truth.

Potential category/taxonomy overlap between the ImageNet-derived category set used for synthetic data generation and evaluation benchmark categories is not discussed, which could inflate apparent 'zero-shot generalization' claims (e.g., for COD transfer).

The paper's core novelty is largely a combination of existing techniques (diffusion feature extraction, concept-attention, DINO features, MHP-style multi-mask decoding, iterative curriculum sampling) rather than a fundamentally new method, which somewhat limits the conceptual contribution despite strong empirical execution.

strengths: Introduces a large-scale (139,981 image) synthetic dataset for salient object detection generated via a novel multi-modal diffusion pipeline that fuses FLUX DiT intermediate features, concept attention maps, and DINO-v3 representations, avoiding reliance on a separate teacher segmentation model.

Iterative, feedback-driven generation strategy that reweights category sampling based on per-category model performance is a sensible and demonstrated-effective (Table 5) mechanism for continual dataset improvement.

Ambiguity-aware multi-mask decoder built on DPT + DINO-v3 is simple yet effective, and the paper provides an honest oracle-vs-non-oracle comparison (S3OD vs S3OD*) to illustrate the residual ambiguity gap.

Extensive experimental evaluation: cross-dataset generalization across six benchmarks, fine-tuned SOTA comparisons, comparisons to other synthetic-data methods (MaskFactory, DatasetDM) under matched data budgets, and multiple ablations (data modalities, iterative rounds, architecture/backbone, prompt engineering, model efficiency).

Reasonable quality-control pipeline (consistency filtering, VLM-based mask/semantic validation) and quantitative synthetic image quality metrics (IS, FID) benchmarked against prior synthetic SOD data generators.
Good coverage and organization of related work situating the contribution relative to pseudo-labeling, diffusion-based segmentation synthesis, and existing SOD architectures.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is unclear: no explicit statement about dataset/code release, generation pipeline hyperparameters (e.g., number of categories, held-out set size for the iterative feedback loop, LLM prompt count per round) are only partially specified.

Cross-dataset generalization comparisons (Table 2) pit S3OD (trained on 139K synthetic images) against baselines trained on much smaller real datasets (DIS, HRSOD-TR, etc.); while Table 4 partially controls for data volume, the headline generalization claims in the abstract/intro (20-50% error reduction) are not clearly disentangled from a pure data-scale effect versus the proposed multi-modal generation method itself.

The architectural contribution (multi-mask decoder with IoU-based branch selection) is a fairly direct application of existing multiple-choice-learning/ambiguity-modeling ideas (Guzman-Rivera et al., Rupprecht et al.) to SOD, limiting novelty on the modeling side; most novelty resides in the data pipeline.

Ablation in Table 6 shows relatively modest differences between using all three modalities versus DINO-v3+DiT alone on several benchmarks, raising questions about whether the added complexity (concept attention maps, fusion module) is fully justified.

Manual quality verification of the dataset is based on only 1,000 randomly sampled masks with no description of annotator qualifications, agreement statistics, or evaluation protocol, limiting confidence in the reported 98.5% quality rate.

No discussion of limitations, failure cases, potential biases inherited from the FLUX diffusion model (e.g., underrepresented object categories, cultural/visual biases), or societal/ethical considerations of relying on purely synthetic training data.

Minor writing/presentation issues (e.g., typos such as 'siginificantly', inconsistent capitalization of dataset name, dense notation in Section 3) reduce clarity and would benefit from another editing pass.
No error bars, variance across seeds, or statistical significance testing are reported for the main results, making it hard to assess whether reported improvements are robust.
